title: 9.1 Small Group · Group 2
contentObjective: I can go beyond today's lesson: plot and identify points on the coordinate plane using ordered pairs in trickier cases, and explain WHY it works.
languageObjective: I can justify my answer to a skeptic and connect it to a second strategy or representation.

noticeAndWonder.context: Three points are plotted on this coordinate grid, all to the right of and above the origin O, where the two number lines cross.

revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Captain Vega’s Treasure Square
revealWordProblem.text: Captain Vega buried treasure at the four corners of a square. Three corners are at (2, 2), (2, 6), and (6, 6). She always plots her corners in Quadrant I. What ordered pair is the fourth corner, and what is the side length of the square?
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: The fourth corner is (6, 2). The square has a side length of 4 units, because from (2, 2) to (6, 2) is 6 − 2 = 4 units and from (2, 2) to (2, 6) is 6 − 2 = 4 units.

turnAndTalk.question: On the coordinate plane, why do we always start at the origin (0, 0) and move sideways before we move up or down to plot a point?
turnAndTalk.kernel: We start at the origin and move along the x-axis first because ___.

stems.en: The first number in (x, y) tells me to move ___.
stems.es: El primer numero en (x, y) me dice que me mueva ___.

stems.en: The second number tells me to move ___.
stems.es: El segundo numero me dice que me mueva ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Student states the x-coordinate is the sideways (horizontal) move and the y-coordinate is the up/down (vertical) move, both starting from the origin.
turnAndTalk.extend: Push students to explain why (3, 5) and (5, 3) land on different points even though they use the same numbers.
extendStems: The order in an ordered pair matters because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: You need to plot (4, 2). Walk your partner through every move you make from the origin, using the words x-axis and y-axis.
turnAndTalk.kernel: Starting at the origin, I first move ___, then I move ___.

stems.en: I move ___ units along the x-axis.
stems.es: Me muevo ___ unidades por el eje x.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Student moves 4 right along the x-axis and 2 up along the y-axis, naming each axis and the origin as the start.
turnAndTalk.extend: Ask students to predict which quadrant the point (4, 2) lands in and justify their answer using the signs of the coordinates.
extendStems: I can tell the quadrant from the coordinates by ___.

turnAndTalk.question: How is reading a coordinate pair like reading directions on a map or in a video game?
turnAndTalk.kernel: An ordered pair works like map directions because ___.

stems.es: La coordenada x es como ir ___.
La coordenada y es como ir ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Student connects the x-value to horizontal travel and the y-value to vertical travel, like map or grid directions from a starting point.
turnAndTalk.extend: Push students to generalize a rule for plotting ANY ordered pair, including ones with zero in them.
extendStems: A rule that always works for plotting (x, y) is ___.
If one coordinate is 0, the point lands on ___ because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: A classmate plotted (2, 6) but moved up 2 and over 6. What mistake did they make, and how would you coach them?
turnAndTalk.kernel: The mistake was ___, and to fix it they should ___.

stems.en: They mixed up the ___ and the ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Student identifies that the x- and y-coordinates were swapped and explains the correct order (x first, then y).
turnAndTalk.extend: Ask students to critique why this swap error is so common and suggest a strategy to avoid it every time.

A strategy to remember the order is ___.

turnAndTalk.question: During practice on Graph on the Coordinate Plane, what strategy did you use when a problem felt tricky?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Always start at the origin (0, 0), move right/left first, then up/down.

stems.en: I move ___ units along the x-axis.
stems.es: Me muevo ___ unidades por el eje x.

stems.en: I knew my answer was reasonable because ___.

launch.narrative: This is your challenge small group for Lesson 9.1. You've got the basics — now let's push on it: harder cases, a second strategy, and always the question "how do you KNOW?"
launch.contextImage: Old parchment treasure map with a coordinate grid overlay and compass rose

Which number tells you how far right/left? Which tells you up/down?
Why is the ORDER in an ordered pair important?

How would you describe a location without a coordinate plane?

conceptIntro.heading: Push further — How do you plot a point on the coordinate plane?
conceptIntro.intro: You already can do this. In this group we go deeper: trickier numbers, a second way to see it, and explaining why it works — not just getting the answer.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Always start at the origin (0, 0), move right/left first, then up/down. — and you can explain WHY, and predict when it gets tricky.

iDo.title: Watch me
lines: I will plot the point (5, 4). The 5 is the x-coordinate, and the 4 is the y-coordinate.
I start at the origin, which is (0, 0).
First I move 5 units to the right along the x-axis.
Then I move 4 units up. I place my dot. That is the point (5, 4).

weDo.title: Generalize it
lines: Start from what you know: Now let's plot (2, 1). Where do we start? At the origin (0, 0).
Now predict: what happens with much bigger numbers, or numbers that share no common factors? Make a prediction, then check it.

onLevel.title: onLevel — Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Move right
workedExample.work: Move 4 units to the right along the x-axis. Good.

workedExample.label: Move up
workedExample.work: Move 4 units up, because the pair has a 4 in it.

onLevel.correctWork: The y-coordinate is 0, not 4. After moving 4 right, the up move is 0 units, so the point stays on the x-axis at (4, 0). The student reused the x-value instead of reading the second number (0).
hints: What is the SECOND number in (4, 0), and how far up does it tell you to move?
A y-coordinate of 0 means do not move up at all — the point sits right on the x-axis at (4, 0).

onLevel.label: Plot these points to reveal a hidden shape: (1, 1), (1, 5), (6, 5), (6, 1)
onLevel.hint: Start at the origin (0, 0) for each point. Move right first, then up.
hints: Each pair is (x, y). For point A(1, 1) both moves are just 1 unit.
For every point: start at (0, 0), slide right x units along the bottom, then climb up y units.
Plot A first: right 1, up 1. Then B(1, 5): same x, so it sits straight above A — count up to 5.

extending.title: Extending — Miscounted Grid Lines

workedExample.label: Move along the x-axis
workedExample.work: Start at the origin (0, 0) and count 7 units to the right.

workedExample.label: Move along the y-axis
workedExample.work: Count up from the x-axis: 1, 2, 3, 4 — stop on 4.

extending.correctWork: The x-axis itself is 0, not 1. Counting up correctly: 1, 2, 3 — the third count lands on y = 3, so the point is (7, 3), not (7, 4). The student started counting one gridline too high by treating the x-axis as unit 1 instead of unit 0.
hints: When you count up from the x-axis, is the x-axis itself unit 0 or unit 1?
The x-axis is 0. The first line above it is 1, the second is 2, the third is 3. So 3 units up lands on y = 3, not y = 4.

extending.prompt: A student says that (3, 5) and (5, 3) are the same point because they use the same numbers. Is the student correct? Explain why or why not, and describe where each point is located on the coordinate plane.
extending.sentenceFrame: The student is ___ because (3, 5) means ___ while (5, 3) means ___. The ORDER matters because ___.
extending.hint: Compare what each coordinate pair tells you about horizontal and vertical moves.
hints: Both pairs use 3 and 5, but look at which number sits in the x (first) spot in each pair.
Describe each point's moves separately: (3, 5) = right ?, up ?; (5, 3) = right ?, up ?. Compare the two paths.
First step: for (3, 5), go right 3 and up 5. Now do (5, 3)'s moves and check whether you land on the same dot.

extending.label: Plot the points (2, 3), (2, 7), (6, 7), (6, 3). Connect them. Name the shape and find its perimeter using the coordinates.
extending.hint: Start at the origin (0, 0) for each point. Move right first, then up.
hints: Plot all 4 points first. Notice A and B share x = 2, and B and C share y = 7 — that makes straight sides.
Count side lengths on the grid, or subtract coordinates: same-x sides use the y-values, same-y sides use the x-values.
Side AB runs from (2, 3) to (2, 7): count 7 − 3 units. Find the other side lengths, then add all four.

optional.stem: Spot 1 — Captain Vega's first clue says the Sandy Dock is right 7 and up 2 from the origin. Which ordered pair names the Sandy Dock?
optional.explanation: The x-coordinate is the sideways move (right 7) and the y-coordinate is the up move (up 2), so the Sandy Dock is (7, 2).
choiceFeedback: You swapped the x and y—the first number is horizontal, second is vertical.
Remember the x-coordinate tells you how far horizontally.
The first number is the horizontal (right/left) distance.

optional.stem: Spot 2 — The map marks the Lookout Tower at (4, 9). What does the 4 tell you to do from the origin?
choices: Move 4 units to the right along the x-axis
Move 4 units up along the y-axis
optional.explanation: The first number in (x, y) is the x-coordinate, so 4 means move 4 units to the right along the x-axis before moving up.
choiceFeedback: The first number controls horizontal movement—check which number moves you up.
With a positive first number, you move right—not left.

optional.stem: Spot 3 — Vega writes: 'The Coconut Grove is 3 across and 8 up.' Which point on the map is the Coconut Grove?
optional.explanation: Across (3) is the x-coordinate and up (8) is the y-coordinate, so the Coconut Grove is at (3, 8).
choiceFeedback: You swapped the x and y—the first number is horizontal, second is vertical.
Double-check: verify the math step-by-step against the question.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Graph on the Coordinate Plane is swapping the order of the coordinates — moving up/down first instead of right/left first. For example, when plotting (5, 2), students often move up 5 and right 2, landing on the wrong point (2, 5) instead of (5, 2). Remember: the x-coordinate (first number) always tells you how far to move right or left along the x-axis; the y-coordinate (second number) tells you how far up or down along the y-axis.

optionalActivity.name: Coordinate Treasure Map
optionalActivity.intro: Challenge — prove it: Read Captain Vega's ordered-pair clues to plot every treasure spot in Quadrant I. Convince a skeptic your answer is right.

diagram.title: Drone Flight Path Triangle
diagram.caption: Each ordered pair (x, y) places a stop: read x for the sideways move, y for the up move — connect Base to Pickup to Delivery and back to see the triangle.

connect.scenario: A drone delivery company programs flight paths using coordinate pairs. A drone starts at the warehouse (0, 0), flies to pickup at (3, 6), then delivers to (8, 2), then returns to base (0, 0).
connect.promptQuestion: How do ordered pairs help the drone navigate? What shape does the flight path make?
connect.prompt: The drone uses ordered pairs because the first number controls ___ movement and the second controls ___. The path makes a ___ shape.

exitTicket.stem: Explain your thinking — Point P is located 6 units right and 3 units up from the origin. What ordered pair names point P?
exitTicket.explanation: Right 6 = x-coordinate of 6, Up 3 = y-coordinate of 3. The ordered pair is (6, 3).
choiceFeedback: You swapped them — the x-coordinate (right) comes first.
The point moved up 3 too — the y-coordinate isn't zero.
It moved right 6 first — the x-coordinate isn't zero.
hints: Point P's moves: 6 right, then 3 up. In an ordered pair the horizontal move is written first.
Build the pair as (x, y) = (right distance, up distance). Match each number to its move before choosing.
Right 6 means the x-coordinate is 6, so the pair starts with 6. Now place the 'up 3' move in its slot.

smallGroup.label: Challenge
smallGroup.who: Pull students who showed mastery on the formative check and are ready to extend.
moves: Launch the challenge fast — skip the re-teach, they don't need it.
Step back. Let them wrestle; protect the productive struggle.
Ask "How do you know?" and "Can you show it a second way?" more than you explain.
Push for a generalization: when does this hold, and when would it break?
Close by having one student justify a claim to the group.
